facts.claim: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The negative-rights/positive-directives distinction is a general textbook comparison, not an absolute rule: some Fundamental Rights impose positive obligations. Directive Principles may be implemented through legislation or executive action. Fundamental Rights generally operate without an implementing law. Statement 3 reverses the sanctions: rights are judicially enforceable, while Directive Principles carry moral and political responsibility under Article 37.

facts.claim: The assertion and reason must distinguish two separate constitutional provisions. Article 37 makes Directive Principles non-justiciable but fundamental in governance. Article 32, in Part III, guarantees the right to approach the Supreme Court to enforce Fundamental Rights. Article 37 does not itself provide the Article 32 remedy.

facts.claim: Minerva Mills invalidated the 42nd Amendment’s expansion of Article 31C to all Directive Principles. It also invalidated the attempted unlimited amending power in Article 368(4) and (5); it did not strike down only section 4 of that Amendment. Article 31C in its constitutionally surviving form protects qualifying Article 39(b) and (c) laws, with judicial review of the necessary connection. Property Owners Association (2024 INSC 835) confirmed that this surviving Article 31C remains in force.

facts.claim: A is true, R is false. Golak Nath treated a constitutional amendment as 'law' under Article 13(2) and held that Parliament could not take away or abridge Fundamental Rights, so they could not be amended to carry out the directives. It applied this prospectively (6.4.1 POL-6.1.9-P129-05, P129-06). The Court said nothing to make Part IV enforceable. Article 37 still bars court enforcement, so R is false. Options 1 and 2 need R to be true. Option 4 reverses the truth values. Parliament answered with the 24th and 25th Amendments (1971), and Kesavananda (1973) reversed Golak Nath's position (card 6.5.2-C02 rows 1967–1973).

Pairs 1 and 3 are correct. Champakam Dorairajan was decided in 1951 and Minerva Mills in 1980. Golak Nath was decided in 1967, not 1971. 1971 is the year of the 24th and 25th Amendments that answered it. Options 1, 2 and 3 all include the wrong pair 2. Fix the line: 1951 Champakam, 1967 Golak Nath, 1971 the 24th and 25th Amendments, 1973 Kesavananda, 1976 the 42nd Amendment, 1980 Minerva Mills (card 6.5.2-C02). The 6.5.1 fact register records the Minerva Mills year as untested (POL-651-P147-minerva).
